builder_plan.scenario: A workflow needs specialist review, but extra agents may add more cost than useful work.
builder_plan.change: Test the proposed division of work against a single-agent implementation.
builder_plan.baseline: One agent with the same tools and an equal total token and time budget.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Accepted outputs, coordination failures, wall-clock time, and total cost across all agents.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: WorkflowArena: Benchmarking Executable Workflow Orchestration in LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems
summary: The benchmark replaces ad hoc evaluation of multi-agent setups—which previously measured only end-to-end task completion or coordination under pre-specified structures—with joint evaluation of deliverable quality and autonomously authored delegation structure. Adopting model-authored workflow orchestration costs additional API calls for delegation, increases system complexity, and adds reliance on frontier models (Opus 5.5, GPT in Codex) that are only available through third-party APIs. It can fail because no single model or configuration performs best across all eight domains, so a delegation strategy that works in software engineering may degrade in legal analysis or 3D production.
rationale: The finding that workflow authorship is a measurable, transferable determinant of performance is relevant to any multi-agent deployment, but the benchmark itself requires frontier API access and per-domain validation before production adoption.
technique: Workflow orchestration benchmark for multi-agent LLM systems

claims.statement: The benchmark replaces ad hoc evaluation of multi-agent setups—which previously measured only end-to-end task completion or coordination under pre-specified structures—with joint evaluation of deliverable quality and autonomously authored delegation structure. Adopting model-authored workflow orchestration costs additional API calls for delegation, increases system complexity, and adds reliance on frontier models (Opus 5.5, GPT in Codex) that are only available through third-party APIs. It can fail because no single model or configuration performs best across all eight domains, so a delegation strategy that works in software engineering may degrade in legal analysis or 3D production.
When the executing model is held fixed on a challenging task subset, workflows authored by Claude Opus 5.5 substantially improve weaker executors; no multiplicative factor is given.
